Write a short blog post about the weather and how it has changed your plans. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
We had meant to start for the lake on Saturday morning. Mr. Stewart had the wagon packed by Friday night, with the tent, the two quilts, the big coffee pot, and a sack of corn meal which he said would be needed whether the fish were biting or not. He is a very careful man about such things, and he had looked at the sky twice before supper and pronounced it "fair enough."

But the sky is a deceitful thing. About four o'clock Saturday morning I woke to a sound on the roof like a handful of peas thrown down, and by daylight the rain was coming in sheets across the yard. The hens stood under the porch looking insulted. The creek, which is usually a thing a child can step across, had made up its mind to be a river, and the little bridge was nowhere to be seen.

Mr. Stewart came in from the barn with water running off his hat brim, and set himself down by the stove. "Wooman," he said, "we'll no be gaeing to the lake the day." I said I had come to that conclusion myself, since I had seen the washtub float by the gate. He did not think that was as funny as I did.

For an hour or so he was very low in spirits. He walked from window to window and tapped the glass as if the weather might be persuaded by it. Then he went out and unpacked the wagon, grumbling at every quilt, and carried the corn meal back to the kitchen, where it was put to use at once, for there is nothing like a disappointed man for eating hot cakes.

Now, I will not say the day was wasted. The rain kept on, and the neighbors, who could not work in the fields either, began to turn up one by one. Old Mr. Hadley came first, wet to the knees, with a fiddle under his coat. Then came the two Pruitt boys, who were sent over, they said, to borrow a lantern, though nobody believed it. By noon we had nine people in the front room, and the big coffee pot, which was to have gone fishing, was doing its duty on the stove.

Mr. Hadley played every tune he knew, and a few he only half knew, and the boys sang the words wrong with great spirit. Mr. Stewart forgot to look at the window at all.

The lake will keep. The fish, I am told, are in no hurry. We have set another Saturday, and he has already looked at the sky twice, but I notice that this time he has not said "fair enough." I think the weather has taught him a little modesty, and that is worth a day's rain.
